title: honest work
hook: honest work; Nanak's three pillars start here

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar, line two: without fear, without hate. Today, the first of three pillars Sikhs build a life on. Day twelve.

A mountaintop. A begging bowl. A cave. The classic pictures of a holy man: someone who gave everything away, or left his family to meditate alone. Guru Nanak, back from his years on the road, chose differently. He spent the rest of his life on a farm by a river, plowing fields, raising a family, growing food. The founder of a faith, with his hands in the dirt.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINTOP. THE BEGGING BOWL.` → `NANAK CHOOSES A FARM.` → `THE FIRST OF THREE PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Kirat karni. Kirat means honest labor, the work of your hands and your head. Karni means to do. So: do honest work. Earn your living, and earn it cleanly. Sikhs often describe daily life as resting on three pillars, and this is the first. In Nanak's day, some seekers left ordinary life behind: work, family and home, living on alms. Nanak honored sincere seekers wherever he met them. But the life he taught was the householder's. You don't have to leave the world to find God; you find God in the middle of it, in the field, in the shop, at the kitchen table. So in his last years, at Kartarpur, the Guru farmed. A line in the scripture sums it up. In paraphrase: the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, recognizes the path. Notice the word honest. Work without cheating, without exploiting anyone, without taking what isn't yours. The first pillar isn't in a temple. It's on Monday morning.
screen: `KIRAT — HONEST LABOR. KARNI — TO DO.` · `NOT LEAVING THE WORLD. LIVING IN IT.` · `THE GURU WHO FARMED.` · `EARNED BY EFFORT, WITHOUT CHEATING.`

segments.voice: Look at your hands for a moment. Think about the work they do: paid work, housework, schoolwork, caring for someone. Pick one piece of it that's coming up, and picture doing it cleanly: no corner cut, nothing taken that isn't yours. Stay with that picture.
Kirat karni. Honest work: earning a living by your own effort, without cheating anyone. The first pillar. Twelfth word.
Your line: earn it clean. The shortcut nobody would notice is exactly where this pillar stands. Day twelve.

howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to live as householders and to earn their living honestly through their own work, and kirat karni is named with sharing and remembering the name as one of the three pillars of Sikh life.

match.prompt: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

myth: Nanak taught that the holiest life means leaving work and family
he taught the householder's life: finding God in the middle of ordinary work.
in his last years, Guru Nanak farmed at Kartarpur
the founder of the faith spent those years working the fields.
kirat karni just means stay busy
it means honest work: without cheating, exploiting or taking what isn't yours.

fork.setup: you're Nanak. after long years on the road, you could live anywhere and be supported by followers. where do you settle?
options: a cave in the mountains, to meditate alone.
a farm by a river, working the land.
fork.reveal: tradition says he settled at Kartarpur and farmed. the first pillar isn't in a temple; it's in the field.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: kirat (honest labor) + karni (to do).

trapdoor: what you thought: have a job.
what it means: earn your living by your own honest effort, without cheating anyone, as part of a spiritual life, not apart from it.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak taught the householder's life rather than renunciation, and a line in the scripture ties earning by effort to giving with your own hand.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (one who eats what they earn by effort and gives some with their own hand recognizes the path)
Sikh tradition on Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur

notes: Ang 1245 line (ghaal khaae kichh hathhu dehi, Nanak raahu pachhaanehi sei) paraphrased and attributed to Guru Nanak; confirm the attribution and Ang.
The three pillars (kirat karni, vand chhakna, naam japna) are a standard modern summary; confirm framing as 'Sikhs often describe'.
The renunciation contrast is phrased without judging other paths ('Nanak honored sincere seekers'); confirm tone.
